headerBody: Australia: Tourist Scams documents 84 specific scams against Australian police and consumer-agency sources — NSW and Victoria Police, the ACCC's Scamwatch service, NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria — plus r/sydney and r/melbourne reports and verified Australian news. The exact scripts, the tells that give them away, and the plain-English phrases that shut them down. Sourced against the record, not recycled from blog lists.
quadHead: Four ways Australia catches tourists off guard.

quad.title: Great Barrier Reef 'Cheap Tour' Bait & Switch
quad.tl: An Esplanade booth sells a 'AUD 99 full-day Great Barrier Reef tour' that actually runs to an inner-reef sandspit with 3–5 m visibility — the genuine outer-reef sites (Agincourt, Flynn, Michaelmas) you imagined cost AUD 220–AUD 300. Ask the exact site name before you pay; anything under AUD 160 is inner-reef.

quad.title: Tullamarine Fake-Taxi Bait
quad.tl: A man in a high-vis vest meets you at baggage claim offering a ride 'cheaper than Uber' and walks you to an unmarked sedan in the carpark — forty minutes later, with the meter hidden under a clipboard, he demands AUD 185 for a trip a real cab runs at AUD 60–AUD 80. Touting inside the terminal is illegal; walk out to the signposted ranks.

quad.title: The Jet-Ski Phantom-Damage Deposit
quad.tl: You hire a jet ski at The Spit — AUD 180 for 30 minutes against a AUD 500 security deposit. At return the operator points to a 'new' scratch on the hull, keeps the full deposit and puts a AUD 750 'repair' charge on your card. Film every panel of the hull on video before you launch and again at handback.

quad.title: Counterfeit BridgeClimb & Opera House Tickets
quad.tl: A man near Cumberland Street offers a last-minute BridgeClimb 'a tourist cancelled' for AUD 80 under the usual AUD 170–AUD 335. You pay cash, he texts a QR code and vanishes — at reception the code is dead and his number is disconnected. There are no authorized third-party resellers; book at bridgeclimb.com and sydneyoperahouse.com only.

body: Australia: Tourist Scams is part of the tabiji.ai Travel Safety Series. Every scam is documented against Australian police and consumer-agency sources — NSW and Victoria Police, the ACCC's Scamwatch service, NSW Fair Trading and Consumer Affairs Victoria, and Transport for NSW — plus r/sydney and r/melbourne reports and verified Australian news. Sourced, not recycled.

84 specific scams across Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Cairns, the Gold Coast and nine more cities. The exact scripts, the red flags that give them away, and the plain-English phrases that shut them down — the lines you can show on your phone, with the steps to lodge a Scamwatch report if it has already happened.
Scams evolve, so the book is re-researched and updated every year — the current edition lives in your Kindle library. Built for the traveler who wants to move through Australia relaxed, not braced.
